She is rigorous, formidably well read and almost entirely uninterested in the social conventions that would make fieldwork easier, which is why she arrives in a remote northern village in October 1909 with excellent research plans and almost no practical arrangements. The novel is written as her own field journal, so the account of events is hers throughout, complete with footnotes. She treats faerie lore as a body of evidence to be tested rather than as superstition, and she is far more comfortable with the Folk's rules than with her own neighbours'.
characters.name: Emily Wilde

characters.description: Emily's dog, an enormous black hound who travels with her to Ljosland. Elderly in his habits and devoted to Emily, he spends most of his time apparently asleep in front of whatever fire is available, and is a good deal more capable than that suggests.
characters.name: Shadow

characters.description: The farmer at Hrafnsvik responsible for the cottage Emily has been lent for the winter. Blunt, unwelcoming and disinclined to explain himself, he regards a visiting scholar as an imposition on the village and has prepared her accommodation accordingly.
characters.name: Krystjan Egilson

characters.description: A leading figure in Hrafnsvik, who takes on the management of the village's relationship with its visiting scholar. Practical, even-handed and patient, she smooths over the offence Emily gives without meaning to, and she is the person Emily can go to for an honest account of local tradition and of the accommodations the village has long made with the Folk.
characters.name: Aud

characters.description: A young man of Hrafnsvik, among the first of the villagers to be openly friendly to Emily rather than merely polite, and willing to answer her questions about what people there believe and what they do about it.
characters.name: Finn

characters.description: A young woman of Hrafnsvik, married to Margret. She is one of the villagers Emily comes to know while collecting accounts of the Folk, and her household, like every household in the village, lives under the long and uneasy arrangement Hrafnsvik has with them.
characters.name: Lilja

characters.description: A young woman of Hrafnsvik, married to Lilja, and more reserved with the visiting scholar than her wife is. Like everyone in the village, she has grown up with the rules that govern living close to the Folk and takes them entirely seriously.
characters.name: Margret

characters.description: A small faerie of the common sort living near Emily's cottage. Emily, who knows the etiquette from her own research, leaves him offerings and is repaid in information and small practical assistances, and he becomes her most reliable local source on the Folk of Ljosland. He is one of the very few relationships in the village that she manages without difficulty, largely because the rules governing it are written down.
characters.name: Poe

characters.description: Emily's colleague and rival at Cambridge: elegant, indolent, extravagantly charming and the author of work she considers thin but enviably popular. He follows her to Ljosland uninvited, arrives comfortable and beautifully dressed in a place that is neither, and within days has won over the entire village that Emily has spent weeks failing with. Emily has long believed, on the strength of accumulated evidence rather than instinct, that he is not human at all but one of the Folk living in exile among mortals, and she keeps careful notes on the question.
characters.name: Wendell Bambleby

characters.description: The ruler of Ljosland's courtly Folk, the power behind the winter and behind everything Hrafnsvik has learned to fear and appease. The village's rules, its offerings and its careful avoidance of certain places all exist to limit how often his people take what they want from it.
characters.name: The King of the Hidden Ones

recaps.ending: Emily brings her involvement with the courtly Folk of Ljosland to a conclusion, recovering what had been taken from Hrafnsvik and ending the danger that had shaped the village's life for generations. Her method throughout is scholarly rather than heroic: she knows the shape of the stories these beings live inside better than they expect a mortal to, and she uses the rules within them. The village that began by resenting her ends by treating her as one of its own, and her encyclopaedia, the work of years, is finished. Wendell Bambleby stops pretending to be a human academic: he is an exiled faerie king, driven out of his own realm by his stepmother, who holds it and has no intention of letting him live to reclaim it. He asks Emily to marry him. She neither accepts nor refuses, and the proposal is left standing. They return to Cambridge together with nothing about his position resolved. He is still exiled, still unable to reach his own realm, and still within reach of the people his stepmother sends, and Emily now has a personal stake in a problem she previously regarded as a fascinating case study. That exile, and the question of whether a door back into his kingdom can be found at all, is what the next book takes up.
recaps.in_short: Emily Wilde, a Cambridge dryadologist compiling the first comprehensive encyclopaedia of faeries, spends the winter of 1909 in Hrafnsvik, a remote village in the northern country of Ljosland, to document the one class of Folk her book still lacks. Brilliant at research and hopeless at people, she alienates most of the village within a week, is rescued from her own impracticality by the villagers' patience, and cultivates a small local faerie named Poe as a source. Her Cambridge rival Wendell Bambleby arrives uninvited and charms everyone effortlessly, confirming Emily's long-held suspicion that he is not human but an exiled faerie king. Investigating Hrafnsvik's losses to the courtly Folk, Emily goes further into their territory than any scholar has, and uses her knowledge of how faerie stories work to recover the villagers who had been taken and end the threat the village has lived under for generations. Her encyclopaedia is completed, the village adopts her, and Bambleby, no longer hiding what he is, asks her to marry him. She gives no answer, and they return to Cambridge with his exile unresolved.

recaps.text: Emily Wilde, a Cambridge dryadologist, arrives in October 1909 at Hrafnsvik, a small village on the northern island country of Ljosland, with her dog Shadow and a plan to spend the winter documenting the local Folk for the encyclopaedia of faeries she has spent years assembling. Ljosland's courtly faeries are found nowhere else and the entry on them is the last gap in her book. The practical side of the expedition goes wrong immediately: the cottage arranged for her is cold and half-provisioned, she cannot manage the stove or the firewood, and her host, a farmer named Krystjan Egilson, plainly regards her as an imposition. Her manner offends much of the village within days. Aud, who effectively speaks for Hrafnsvik, takes over the management of the relationship, and Emily begins collecting the villagers' accounts of the Folk and of the strict local rules for living alongside them.

Emily's fieldwork settles into a routine of interviews in the village, expeditions into the surrounding country, and close observation of the small common faeries near her cottage, including one she names Poe, whom she cultivates with offerings until he becomes a genuine source. She learns how much Hrafnsvik has lost to the Folk over the years and how seriously its precautions are taken by people who do not regard them as folklore. Then Wendell Bambleby, her Cambridge colleague and academic rival, arrives uninvited, comfortable, elegantly dressed and instantly popular with everyone Emily has been struggling to get on with. Her private suspicion about him, that he is not a human scholar at all but one of the Folk living in exile, hardens as she watches him in a place where the Folk are close at hand.

Working with and around Bambleby, Emily gets closer to Ljosland's courtly Folk than any scholar before her and closer than the village considers remotely wise. She establishes that Hrafnsvik's losses are not old history: people have been taken within living memory, and at least one who came back did not come back as themselves. Emily approaches this as a scholar. The traditional tales are data, and the rules inside them describe how the Folk can be bound, bargained with and outmanoeuvred, so she begins using what she knows on the village's behalf rather than only recording it. Her running observations of Bambleby accumulate at the same time, and in a country where the Folk are close at hand he grows steadily less careful about what he lets her see.

Emily's involvement with the courtly Folk becomes direct and dangerous. She crosses into their territory, where the ordinary rules of distance and time do not hold, in order to recover what has been taken from Hrafnsvik, and finds the king who rules Ljosland's Folk at the centre of the village's long misfortune. Her one advantage is that she knows the shape of the stories these beings live inside better than they expect a mortal to, and she plays it deliberately. Bambleby, meanwhile, stops troubling to hide from Emily what she had already concluded he was. He is one of the Folk himself, an exiled faerie king; his exile was not chosen, his stepmother holds his kingdom, and she has no intention of letting him survive to take it back.

Emily brings the confrontation with Ljosland's Folk to a conclusion, recovering the villagers who had been taken and ending the danger that had shaped Hrafnsvik for generations. The village that began by resenting her ends by counting her as one of its own, and her encyclopaedia, the work of years, is finally complete. Bambleby, no longer pretending to be anything other than what he is, asks Emily to marry him. She neither accepts nor refuses and the proposal is left open. They return to Cambridge with his situation entirely unresolved: he is still exiled, still cut off from his own realm, and still within reach of the people his stepmother sends after him, and finding a way back into his kingdom is the problem the next book takes up.

characters.description: A Cambridge dryadologist, now the author of the first comprehensive encyclopaedia of faeries and a scholar of established reputation, which has improved her standing at the university without making academic politics any easier for her. She remains rigorous, blunt and far more fluent in the rules of the Folk than in those of her own species. The book is again written as her field journal. She begins it with a marriage proposal from a faerie king outstanding and unanswered, and with a research problem she has not admitted is personal.
characters.name: Emily Wilde

characters.description: Emily's colleague at Cambridge and, as of the previous book, openly what she long suspected: an exiled faerie king, driven out of his own realm by his stepmother. Charming, indolent, beautifully dressed and disinclined to take his own danger seriously, he continues teaching and continues pressing the proposal Emily has not answered. Being cut off from his own realm is a worse problem for him than he lets on.
characters.name: Wendell Bambleby

characters.description: Emily's dog, an enormous black hound, older now and no less devoted, who accompanies her out of Cambridge again.
characters.name: Shadow

characters.description: Emily's niece, newly arrived to work as her assistant. Young, enthusiastic, determined to become a dryadologist herself, and a great deal more socially fluent than her aunt, she is undeterred by Emily's manner and inclined to treat obvious danger as an academic opportunity.
characters.name: Ariadne Wilde

characters.description: The faerie queen who holds Wendell's kingdom, having driven him out of it, and who has gone on sending people after him in the mortal world since. She is known quantity rather than mystery at the start of this book: she wants him dead, and she has both the reach and the patience to keep trying.
characters.name: Wendell's Stepmother

characters.description: The small faerie Emily befriended in Hrafnsvik, who has attached himself to her and followed her back to Cambridge. He is out of his native country and disinclined to leave her household regardless.
characters.name: Poe

characters.description: A senior dryadologist of considerable reputation and rigid views, long retired from fieldwork. He is sceptical of Emily's conclusions, disapproving of her methods, and openly distrustful of Wendell Bambleby for reasons he is not initially willing to spell out.
characters.name: Farris Rose

characters.description: A celebrated dryadologist of an earlier generation who vanished decades ago in the course of her research into the doors between the mortal world and the realms of the Folk. Her reputation was formidable and her disappearance never explained. Her surviving papers, and the map she was said to have made, are the starting point for Emily's search.
characters.name: Danielle de Grey

recaps.ending: Emily finds the door, and the party reaches Wendell's realm. Wendell takes back his throne and his stepmother's hold on the kingdom is broken, but the victory is spoiled at once: she has poisoned the land itself, and the realm is sick and dying in a way that simply reclaiming it does not fix. Because a faerie king and his kingdom are not separable things, that sickness is also Wendell's, so the problem he spent two books trying to solve turns out to have been the easy half. Emily, who has spent two books declining to answer him, accepts his proposal and with it the position that comes attached to it. Danielle de Grey's fate is settled and her work is finally in the hands of someone able to use it, and Ariadne has her fieldwork and rather more of it than she bargained for. Farris Rose's objections have been overtaken by events. The book closes with Emily in a faerie kingdom rather than in Cambridge, no longer a visiting scholar of the Folk but a resident of their world with a title, and with her scholarship pointed at a problem no dryadologist has ever had access to: how to heal a poisoned faerie realm before it takes its king with it.
recaps.in_short: Back at Cambridge with her encyclopaedia published, Emily Wilde takes on a new problem: Wendell Bambleby, now openly an exiled faerie king, cannot return to his own realm, his stepmother's agents can still reach him, and the exile is doing him real harm. Emily's answer is research. She begins reconstructing the work of Danielle de Grey, a dryadologist who vanished decades earlier while studying the doors between worlds, on the theory that de Grey's lost map could locate a way into Wendell's kingdom. The search takes Emily, Wendell, her niece Ariadne and the sceptical senior scholar Farris Rose into the Austrian Alps, to a village living under severe rules alongside its own Folk. The expedition is attacked, Wendell's health fails, and Emily crosses into faerie territory in pursuit of de Grey's route. She finds de Grey herself, still alive inside a faerie realm, and with what she knows the door becomes findable. Wendell reclaims his throne, but his stepmother has poisoned the land, which is dying. Emily accepts his proposal and stays.

recaps.text: Previously: Emily Wilde, a Cambridge dryadologist, spent the winter of 1909 in Hrafnsvik, a remote village in the northern country of Ljosland, gathering the last material for her encyclopaedia of faeries. Socially disastrous and academically formidable, she won the village over slowly, cultivated a small local faerie named Poe as a source, and got closer to Ljosland's courtly Folk than any scholar before her. Her Cambridge rival Wendell Bambleby followed her there uninvited, and she confirmed what she had long suspected: he is not human but an exiled faerie king, driven from his own realm by his stepmother, who holds it and wants him dead. Emily dealt with the Folk who had been taking people from the village and recovered those they had taken, and her encyclopaedia was completed. Wendell, no longer hiding what he is, asked her to marry him; she gave no answer, and the proposal was left standing. They returned to Cambridge with his exile unresolved, which is where this book begins.

Emily is back at Cambridge with her encyclopaedia published and her reputation made, and finds academic life no easier for it. Her niece Ariadne joins her as an assistant, ambitious and entirely undeterred by her aunt's manner, and Poe, the faerie from Hrafnsvik, has attached himself to the household. Wendell's proposal remains unanswered, and his situation is worse than he is willing to admit: he cannot return to his own realm, his stepmother's people can still reach him in the mortal world, and being severed from his kingdom is doing him harm. Emily's response is characteristically scholarly. She begins reconstructing the work of Danielle de Grey, a dryadologist of the previous generation who disappeared while investigating the doors between the worlds, on the theory that de Grey's lost map could locate a way into Wendell's realm.

The search takes Emily, Wendell and Ariadne out of Cambridge and into the Austrian Alps, to a mountain village that lives alongside its own local Folk under its own severe set of rules, and where de Grey was last known to have worked. Farris Rose, a senior dryadologist deeply sceptical of Emily's conclusions and of Wendell personally, attaches himself to the expedition. The mountain Folk prove less accommodating than the ones Emily studied in Ljosland, and the villagers' precautions are correspondingly strict. Emily works through de Grey's surviving notes and the local tales in parallel, on the principle that a door will be described in a story long before anyone writes a paper about it.

The work becomes dangerous. The party is attacked, and it becomes clear that the mountains are not the only threat: Wendell's stepmother's interest has followed them, and there is faerie attention on what Emily is trying to find that has nothing to do with scholarship. Wendell's condition deteriorates, and Emily has to face the fact that his exile is not merely a political inconvenience but something that is killing him. She and Ariadne cross into faerie territory in pursuit of de Grey's route, where distance and time behave by their own rules, and Emily's method of reading the Folk through their stories is what keeps them alive there.

Emily establishes what became of Danielle de Grey. She did not simply die in the mountains: Emily finds her alive inside a faerie realm where the ordinary passage of time does not apply, decades after she disappeared. What de Grey knows about the doors between the worlds is the missing piece of Emily's reconstruction, and with it the location of a way into Wendell's realm stops being a rumour and becomes a solvable problem. The expedition turns from research into a race, since Wendell is failing and his stepmother's people have every reason to reach the door first.

Emily finds the door and the party goes through into Wendell's realm. Wendell takes back his throne and breaks his stepmother's hold on the kingdom, but the victory is immediately spoiled: she has poisoned the land itself, and the realm is sick and dying in a way that reclaiming it does not remedy, which means Wendell is too, since a faerie king and his kingdom are not separable things. Emily, having spent two books declining to answer him, accepts his proposal and the position that comes with it. The book closes with her living in a faerie kingdom rather than in Cambridge, and with her scholarship redirected at a problem no dryadologist has ever had access to: how to heal a poisoned faerie realm.

characters.description: A wealthy, clever young woman who lives at Hartfield with her father. Secure in her position and with no need to marry, she enjoys managing the social lives of others and believes she arranged her former governess's successful match.
characters.name: Emma Woodhouse

characters.description: Emma's elderly father, affectionate, anxious, and devoted to familiar routines. He worries about health, travel, rich food, and any marriage that removes a companion from his immediate circle.
characters.name: Mr Woodhouse

characters.description: Emma's former governess and closest maternal friend, newly married to Mr Weston. Gentle and sensible, she remains part of Emma's daily life despite leaving Hartfield.
characters.name: Mrs Weston

characters.description: A prosperous landowner from nearby Donwell Abbey and an old family friend. Direct, perceptive, and willing to challenge Emma, he doubts her claim that she engineered the Westons' marriage.
characters.name: Mr Knightley

characters.description: Mrs Weston's cheerful husband and the father of Frank Churchill from an earlier marriage. Sociable and optimistic, he hopes his son will soon visit Highbury.
characters.name: Mr Weston

characters.description: A pretty, good-tempered seventeen-year-old of uncertain parentage who boards at Mrs Goddard's school. She is flattered by Emma's attention and eager to become her friend.
characters.name: Harriet Smith

characters.description: The young vicar of Highbury, polished and attentive. He is a regular and welcome member of the Woodhouses' social circle.
characters.name: Mr Elton

characters.description: A respectable young tenant farmer on Mr Knightley's estate. Harriet knows him through his sisters and speaks warmly of his capable, good-natured character.
characters.name: Robert Martin

characters.description: A kind but incessantly talkative unmarried woman of reduced means. She lives with her elderly mother, is grateful for every small kindness, and speaks proudly of her accomplished niece Jane Fairfax.
characters.name: Miss Bates

characters.description: Mr Weston's son, raised by his wealthy Churchill relatives and long expected in Highbury. His repeated failure to visit is attributed to the demands of the aunt on whom his prospects depend.
characters.name: Frank Churchill

characters.description: Miss Bates's elegant and highly accomplished niece, orphaned and brought up with the Campbell family. She returns to Highbury before she must seek work as a governess, and Emma feels both curiosity and rivalry toward her.
characters.name: Jane Fairfax

characters.description: Mr Elton's new wife, formerly Augusta Hawkins of Bath. Rich, self-important, and eager to establish her social consequence, she assumes an immediate familiarity with Highbury society.
characters.name: Mrs Elton

recaps.ending: Frank Churchill and Jane Fairfax's secret engagement becomes public after Mrs Churchill dies, freeing Frank from dependence on her approval. Emma recognizes how thoroughly she misread their conduct and is relieved to discover that she never loved Frank. Harriet then reveals that the man she hopes to marry is Mr Knightley. This shocks Emma into realizing that she loves Knightley herself. Knightley, believing Emma distressed over Frank, comes to comfort her and instead proposes; she accepts. Harriet briefly withdraws, then reconciles with Emma after Robert Martin proposes again and she accepts him. Jane and Frank prepare to marry once family arrangements permit. Because Mr Woodhouse cannot bear Emma's departure, Knightley agrees to live at Hartfield after their marriage. A local poultry theft helps persuade Mr Woodhouse that another man in the house is desirable. Emma and Knightley marry, with their equality and long knowledge of one another replacing Emma's earlier fantasies about directing other people's lives.
recaps.in_short: Emma Woodhouse, wealthy and confident in her judgment, befriends Harriet Smith and tries to raise her socially. She persuades Harriet to refuse the farmer Robert Martin and imagines that Mr Elton loves her, only to discover that Elton wants Emma herself. Emma next entertains a flirtation with Frank Churchill while disliking the reserved Jane Fairfax. Her guesses repeatedly mislead her: Frank and Jane are secretly engaged, and his attentions to Emma disguise their relationship. After Emma cruelly jokes at Miss Bates's expense, Mr Knightley's rebuke forces her to confront her selfishness. Harriet's admission that she loves Knightley finally reveals Emma's own love for him. Knightley proposes to Emma, while Harriet accepts a renewed proposal from Robert Martin. Frank and Jane are reconciled and prepare to marry. Knightley moves to Hartfield so Emma need not abandon her anxious father, and Emma's marriage rests on greater humility and self-knowledge.

recaps.text: Emma Woodhouse's former governess, Miss Taylor, marries Mr Weston, leaving Emma and her anxious father alone at Hartfield. Emma claims credit for the match and decides she has a talent for matchmaking, though Mr Knightley warns her against interfering. She befriends Harriet Smith, a pretty boarder of uncertain parentage, and convinces herself that Harriet must be the unacknowledged daughter of a gentleman. When the respectable farmer Robert Martin proposes to Harriet, Emma guides her toward refusal because she considers him socially beneath her. Emma instead imagines a match between Harriet and the local vicar, Mr Elton. She encourages Harriet to interpret his attentions, charitable riddle, and eagerness for company as signs of love.

Emma continues constructing evidence that Mr Elton loves Harriet, although his compliments and attentions are actually directed toward Emma. Mr Knightley learns of Robert Martin's rejection and angrily tells Emma that Harriet has refused an excellent match on her advice. At Christmas, Harriet is ill and cannot join a party at the Westons'. On the carriage ride home, Elton proposes passionately to Emma and dismisses the idea of marrying Harriet as absurd. Emma refuses him and realizes that her vanity caused her to misread everything. Elton leaves Highbury. Emma must tell Harriet the truth and accepts some blame, but she still does not fully question her habit of arranging other people's futures.

Jane Fairfax returns to stay with Miss Bates. Beautiful, reserved, and accomplished, she faces eventual employment as a governess because she has no fortune. Emma remains cool toward her and invents a theory that Jane once loved her friend's married brother-in-law. Frank Churchill finally visits Highbury and quickly charms Emma. He encourages her guesses about Jane and helps plan a ball, while paying conspicuous attention to Emma. A pianoforte arrives anonymously for Jane, feeding speculation about a secret admirer. Emma enjoys Frank's company and briefly thinks she may be in love, though her feelings lack depth. Frank abruptly leaves when his demanding aunt summons him, and the planned ball is postponed.

Mr Elton returns with his bride, Augusta, whose vanity and officiousness quickly irritate Emma. Mrs Elton decides to patronize Jane and presses her to accept a governess position. Frank returns, and the Westons' ball is finally held. Mr Elton pointedly refuses to dance with Harriet, humiliating her, until Mr Knightley asks her to dance. Soon afterward Frank rescues Harriet from a group of troublesome children. Harriet declares that she has put aside her former attachment and now admires a man socially above her. Emma assumes she means Frank and again encourages hope without asking for a name. At the same time, Frank's teasing conduct toward Jane and Emma continues to conceal more than Emma understands.

At an outing to Box Hill, the party is strained and listless. Urged by Frank to entertain everyone, Emma makes a cutting joke at Miss Bates's expense. Mr Knightley privately rebukes her for humiliating a poor, dependent woman who has always treated her kindly. Ashamed, Emma visits Miss Bates the next morning to make amends. Jane, meanwhile, has accepted a governess position and seems distressed; Frank leaves suddenly after an argument. News then arrives that Mrs Churchill has died. With her opposition removed, Frank can disclose that he and Jane have long been secretly engaged. Their quarrels, the anonymous piano, and Frank's flirtation with Emma were all connected to hiding the engagement. Emma is startled by her errors but realizes she does not love Frank.

Harriet tells Emma that her new hope is not Frank Churchill but Mr Knightley. Faced with the possibility of losing him, Emma finally recognizes her own love. Knightley returns to comfort her, believing she is hurt by Frank's engagement, and confesses that he loves her. Emma accepts his proposal. She worries about Harriet and about leaving her father, so Knightley offers to move into Hartfield. Harriet spends time away with Emma's sister, reconnects with Robert Martin, and accepts his renewed proposal; Emma also learns that Harriet's father is a respectable tradesman, not a hidden aristocrat. Frank and Jane reconcile and plan their marriage. After a poultry theft makes Mr Woodhouse more receptive to Knightley's presence, Emma and Knightley marry, and Emma enters the match with a more honest view of her own limitations.

characters.description: A wealthy, clever young woman who manages her father's home at Hartfield and has rarely been contradicted. The marriage of her former governess, Miss Taylor, convinces Emma that she has a talent for arranging other people's happiness. Affectionate and energetic but overconfident in her judgment, she decides to find another match rather than consider marriage for herself.
characters.name: Emma Woodhouse

characters.description: Emma's elderly father, a gentle and devoted man whose fear of illness, rich food, travel, and almost any change shapes life at Hartfield. He regrets Miss Taylor's marriage because it alters his comfortable routine, though he bears no ill will toward her husband.
characters.name: Mr. Woodhouse

characters.description: A close family friend and neighbor from Donwell Abbey. Sensible, observant, and willing to challenge Emma when others indulge her, he doubts her claim that she arranged Miss Taylor's marriage and warns against treating people's lives as a game.
characters.name: Mr. Knightley

characters.description: Emma's former governess and longtime companion, newly married to Mr. Weston. Warm, tactful, and accustomed to Emma's faults as well as her good qualities, she remains Emma's trusted confidante after moving from Hartfield to Randalls.
characters.name: Mrs. Weston

characters.description: Mrs. Weston's cheerful new husband and the owner of Randalls. A sociable widower, he has a grown son from his first marriage who was brought up by wealthy relatives and has not yet visited his father's new home.
characters.name: Mr. Weston

characters.description: A pretty, friendly boarding pupil at Mrs. Goddard's school whose parentage is unknown. Emma is attracted by Harriet's admiration and pliable nature, takes her up as a companion, and begins trying to refine both her social circle and her romantic expectations.
characters.name: Harriet Smith

characters.description: The young clergyman of Highbury, polished and attentive in company. Emma decides that he would make a better husband for Harriet than the farmer Harriet already admires, and she interprets his interest in Emma's plans as encouragement for the match.
characters.name: Mr. Elton

characters.description: A good-hearted but incessantly talkative unmarried woman of limited means, living with her elderly mother. She is welcomed throughout Highbury because of her kindness and good humor, and she speaks proudly and often of her absent niece, Jane Fairfax.
characters.name: Miss Bates

characters.description: A capable young tenant farmer at Abbey-Mill and a friend of Mr. Knightley. Harriet knows and admires his family, and he writes her a sincere proposal of marriage. Emma judges his social position too low for the future she imagines for Harriet.
characters.name: Robert Martin

characters.description: Emma's affectionate elder sister, married to John Knightley and living in London with their children. Gentle and family-minded, she shares her father's anxious concern about health and is happiest when the Hartfield and Knightley households are together.
characters.name: Isabella Knightley

characters.description: Mr. Knightley's younger brother and Isabella's husband. Intelligent, reserved, and strongly attached to domestic life, he visits Hartfield with his wife and children and has little patience for unnecessary social obligations.
characters.name: John Knightley

characters.description: Miss Bates's orphaned niece, recently returned to Highbury after being raised and educated with the Campbell family. Beautiful, highly accomplished, and reserved, she has little money and expects eventually to support herself as a governess. Emma respects her abilities but finds intimacy with her difficult.
characters.name: Jane Fairfax

characters.description: Mr. Weston's son from his first marriage, raised as the heir of his wealthy aunt and uncle, the Churchills. His long-promised visit to Highbury has often been delayed, but when he finally arrives he is lively, charming, and eager to please his father's friends.
characters.name: Frank Churchill

characters.description: Mr. Elton's new wife, formerly Miss Hawkins of Bath. Confident, talkative, and impressed by wealth and social consequence, she quickly speaks to Emma with unwelcome familiarity and presents herself as an important addition to Highbury society.
characters.name: Mrs. Elton

recaps.ending: Frank Churchill's explanatory letter confirms that he and Jane Fairfax had been secretly engaged throughout his stay in Highbury. His apparent courtship of Emma helped conceal the relationship, while his aunt's opposition made secrecy seem necessary. Emma and Jane reconcile, and Jane can now marry Frank because Mrs. Churchill's death has removed the chief obstacle. Emma accepts Mr. Knightley's proposal, but concern for Mr. Woodhouse prevents her from leaving Hartfield; Knightley agrees to live there after their marriage. Harriet spends time in London, recovers from her hopes of Knightley, and renews her connection with Robert Martin. She accepts Martin's second proposal, satisfying Knightley and finally convincing Emma that the match is right. Mrs. Weston gives birth to a daughter. After a nearby poultry theft makes Mr. Woodhouse more receptive to Knightley's protection at Hartfield, he consents to the wedding. Harriet and Robert marry first, and Emma and Knightley then marry with their families and friends in agreement.
recaps.in_short: Emma Woodhouse, a wealthy young woman certain of her insight into others, befriends Harriet Smith and discourages her from marrying the farmer Robert Martin. Emma instead imagines that Mr. Elton loves Harriet, only to discover that he wants Emma herself. After rejecting him, she turns her attention to Frank Churchill, whose flirtation distracts her from his secret engagement to Jane Fairfax. Emma repeatedly misreads Harriet's feelings as well, first believing Harriet attached to Frank and then learning that Harriet hopes to marry Mr. Knightley. This shock makes Emma recognize her own love for Knightley. Her growth is sharpened when he rebukes her for humiliating the kind but vulnerable Miss Bates at Box Hill. Frank and Jane's engagement becomes public after his controlling aunt dies. Knightley proposes to Emma and she accepts. Harriet reunites with Robert Martin and accepts his second proposal, while Knightley agrees to live at Hartfield so Emma need not abandon her anxious father. The novel closes with both couples married and Emma's confidence tempered by greater humility and self-knowledge.

recaps.text: Emma Woodhouse lives comfortably at Hartfield with her anxious, elderly father. Her beloved former governess, Miss Taylor, has just married the sociable widower Mr. Weston, and Emma takes credit for having encouraged the match. Mr. Knightley, a candid family friend from Donwell Abbey, doubts her supposed skill and warns her against further matchmaking. Emma soon befriends Harriet Smith, a pretty and impressionable pupil at Mrs. Goddard's school whose family background is unknown. Although Harriet admires Robert Martin, a respectable young farmer, Emma thinks he is beneath her and imagines a more elevated future for her friend. She chooses the local clergyman, Mr. Elton, as a prospective husband for Harriet and interprets his interest in Emma's portrait of Harriet as proof of affection. When Robert sends Harriet a marriage proposal, Harriet turns to Emma for advice. Emma steers her toward refusal while preserving the appearance that the decision is Harriet's own.

Emma has persuaded Harriet Smith to reject Robert Martin and tries to direct her feelings toward Mr. Elton. Mr. Knightley is angered by the refusal, arguing that Robert is intelligent, honorable, and a very good match for Harriet. Emma remains certain that Elton's attentions are meant for her friend, even when his compliments and eagerness repeatedly center on Emma herself. During the Christmas visit of Emma's sister Isabella and her husband, John Knightley, bad weather disrupts a party at Randalls. Harriet is absent because of illness, and Emma rides home alone with Elton. He proposes passionately to Emma and dismisses the idea of marrying Harriet as socially absurd. Shocked, Emma rejects him and realizes that she has mistaken his conduct from the beginning. Elton, embarrassed and resentful, leaves Highbury for Bath. Emma must now face both the injury her interference has done to Harriet's prospects and the unpleasant task of explaining that Elton never loved Harriet.

Emma explains Mr. Elton's proposal to Harriet, who is deeply hurt, and recognizes that her confident matchmaking has failed. Elton soon becomes engaged elsewhere. Meanwhile Jane Fairfax, the accomplished but poor niece of Miss Bates, returns to Highbury. Orphaned young and educated with the Campbell family, Jane expects eventually to work as a governess. Emma admires her talents but remains uneasy with her reserve and speculates, without evidence, about Jane's friendship with the newly married Mr. Dixon. Frank Churchill, Mr. Weston's son, finally makes his long-delayed visit. Raised by his wealthy and demanding Churchill relatives, Frank is handsome, lively, and immediately attentive to Emma. His willingness to travel to London merely for a haircut strikes Mr. Knightley as frivolous, but Emma enjoys his company as they visit Highbury together. With Elton absent and Frank now present, Emma's attention shifts away from her earlier mistake and toward the possibility of a new romance, while Jane's private feelings remain obscure to her.

After misleading Harriet about Mr. Elton, Emma has begun to question her judgment but continues drawing conclusions about other people's attachments. Jane Fairfax has returned to Highbury with few financial prospects, and Frank Churchill has arrived after many delays. Frank openly enjoys Emma's company, while Emma entertains suspicions about Jane and Mr. Dixon. At a dinner given by the Coles, Jane receives an expensive pianoforte from an unknown giver. Emma and Frank privately treat Mr. Dixon as the likely source, although Jane gives them no support. Frank and Emma flirt and plan for a ball at the Crown, but his aunt summons him away and the event is postponed. Emma decides that she is not truly in love with him, though she thinks his feelings for her may be stronger. Mr. Elton returns with his bride, Augusta. Mrs. Elton is wealthy, self-important, and eager to establish her social authority. She adopts a patronizing interest in Jane and treats Emma with an intimacy Emma dislikes. Mr. Knightley resists Emma's attempts to involve him in her speculations, particularly her suggestion that he might care for Jane.

Emma's first plan for Harriet ended with Mr. Elton proposing to Emma instead and then marrying Augusta Hawkins. Jane Fairfax and Frank Churchill have both come to Highbury, and Emma has misread their guarded behavior while accepting Frank's apparent interest in herself. When Frank returns, the delayed ball at the Crown finally takes place. Mr. Elton pointedly refuses to dance with Harriet, humiliating her, but Mr. Knightley steps forward as her partner and earns Emma's gratitude. Soon afterward Frank helps Harriet escape a frightening encounter with a group of children on the road. Harriet then tells Emma that she has transferred her hopes from Elton to a man far above him; Emma assumes she means Frank and encourages the attachment without asking his name. Mr. Knightley, meanwhile, suspects a private understanding between Frank and Jane, but Emma dismisses the idea. At a gathering at Donwell Abbey, Jane is distressed by Mrs. Elton's efforts to arrange a governess position for her, Frank behaves restlessly, and the tensions Emma has failed to understand become increasingly visible.

Emma continues to believe Harriet has fallen in love with Frank Churchill, while Mr. Knightley suspects that Frank and Jane Fairfax share a secret. During the excursion to Box Hill, Emma joins Frank's careless joking and insults Miss Bates, whose limited circumstances make the public slight especially cruel. Knightley privately rebukes Emma. Ashamed, she visits Miss Bates the next morning to make amends and begins to see how thoughtlessly she has used her social position. Frank leaves suddenly, Jane accepts a governess post, and then Mrs. Churchill dies. With his aunt's opposition removed, Frank's secret engagement to Jane is revealed. Emma is surprised but not heartbroken, because she never truly loved him. She tells Harriet the news, expecting to console her, only to learn that Harriet's admired gentleman is Mr. Knightley, not Frank. Faced with the possibility that Knightley might marry Harriet, Emma finally understands that she loves him herself. Knightley returns from London believing Emma has been wounded by Frank. Their conversation clears away that misunderstanding, and he proposes to Emma. She accepts, though concern for Harriet tempers her happiness.

Emma Woodhouse's efforts to arrange Harriet Smith's future have repeatedly exposed the limits of her judgment. She first discouraged Harriet from accepting Robert Martin and wrongly imagined Mr. Elton in love with Harriet; later she mistook Frank Churchill's flirtation for possible courtship and assumed Harriet loved Frank. At Box Hill, Mr. Knightley's rebuke after Emma insults Miss Bates prompts genuine remorse. Frank's secret engagement to Jane Fairfax then becomes public, and Harriet reveals that she actually hopes to marry Knightley. The shock makes Emma recognize her own love for him. Knightley proposes, and Emma accepts. Frank's letter explains how his dependence on Mrs. Churchill led him and Jane to hide their engagement and how he used attention to Emma as cover. Emma and Jane reconcile. To avoid distressing Mr. Woodhouse, Knightley agrees that after marriage he will move into Hartfield rather than take Emma away. Harriet spends time with Isabella's family in London, reconnects with Robert, and accepts his renewed proposal. Mrs. Weston gives birth to a daughter. A nearby theft helps overcome Mr. Woodhouse's resistance to change, and he consents to Emma's wedding. Harriet and Robert marry, followed by Emma and Knightley.
